practical.title: Your First C Program: Hello, World! (Personalized Greeting)
practical.sourceActivity: Your First C Program: Hello, World! (Personalized Greeting)

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Observe the Starter Program and Run It
teachingPlaylist.description: Compile and run greeting.c to see the original Hello, World! output and learn what each line does.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Be able to identify #include, main, printf, \n, and return 0; and run the compile-run cycle.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Let's compile greeting.c. I'll say each symbol aloud: hash include less-than s t d i o dot h greater-than. Then int main open-parenthesis void close-parenthesis. When you run the compiled program you'll see Hello, World! and a newline. Notice the semicolon ending the printf statement.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Run: clang greeting.c -o greeting then ./greeting. Expected: Hello, World! on its own line.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You found a file greeting.c in your working directory and want to confirm it runs as expected.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the compile and run commands now and tell me whether the output contains Hello, World! and whether the prompt is on the next line.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting to compile first, or mis-typing the file name (case matters).
teachingPlaylist.recap: You confirmed the program compiles and prints Hello, World!. You identified the key language elements.
codeSteps: Read each line aloud and point to punctuation

teachingPlaylist.title: Modify the printf to a Personalized Greeting
teachingPlaylist.description: Change only the string literal in printf to a custom message and observe the effect; then experiment with \n removal.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Make a small change in source code and see its immediate effect on program output.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Edit the printf line, keeping the double quotes and the semicolon. Try: printf open-parenthesis double-quote Hello comma space Cohortia Learner exclamation backslash n double-quote close-parenthesis semicolon. Compile and run. Then remove backslash n, recompile, and observe how the shell prompt behaves.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Modified line: printf("Hello, Cohortia Learner!\n"); Compile and run to see the new message.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You want to personalize the program to verify you understand string literals and escape sequences.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Change the string, compile, run, then remove the \n, recompile and notice where the shell prompt appears.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Removing or altering the double quotes or forgetting the semicolon.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You learned how string literals control terminal output and how \n affects cursor placement.
codeSteps: Edit greeting.c: replace content inside printf double quotes
Remove the \n, recompile, and run to compare

teachingPlaylist.title: Use a Name Variable and %s Format Specifier
teachingPlaylist.description: Introduce a const char *name variable and use printf with %s to print the name from a variable.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand how format specifiers let you insert variables into output strings.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Add a line like const char star name equals double-quote your name double-quote semicolon, then call printf with a format string containing percent s and pass name as a second argument. Compile and run. You should see the greeting that uses the variable's value.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You want to separate data (the name) from the format, practicing formatted printing.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Add the variable and formatted printf, recompile, and observe the same greeting now built from a variable.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Using %d or another wrong format specifier for a string; forgetting to pass name as an argument.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You practiced declaring a string variable and using %s in printf to insert its value.
codeSteps: Edit greeting.c to add: const char *name = "Your Name";

teachingPlaylist.title: Read Compiler Messages and Extend the Program
teachingPlaylist.description: Intentionally remove a semicolon to produce a compiler error, learn to read the message, fix the code, and then extend the greeting.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Be able to interpret a basic compiler error and recover, and to extend the simple program.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Remove the semicolon at the end of the printf line and run clang. The compiler will show an error referencing expected ';' or an unexpected token near return. Read that message, fix the semicolon, and recompile. Optionally, add another printf to print a second line.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: After removing semicolon and running clang, saw: error: expected ';' before 'return'. Restored semicolon and program compiled fine.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You made a small syntax error and need to learn how to fix it based on compiler feedback.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Create the error intentionally, run clang, read the first error lines, then fix and re-run until compilation succeeds.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Reading only part of the error message — read the first few lines; they usually contain the key clue.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You practiced reading a compiler error, fixed the code, and optionally extended the greeting.
codeSteps: Temporarily remove the semicolon from the printf line
Run clang greeting.c -o greeting and read the error
Optional: add another printf to show two lines

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand (2–4 min)
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: We'll compile and run the included greeting.c to observe what it prints. Observe: Notice the include line for standard input/output, the main function header, the printf call and the newline escape sequence \n, and the return 0; statement. Change: You won't change the file yet — just run it. Test: Compile with clang greeting.c -o greeting then run ./greeting and see output. Explain: If you see Hello, World! followed by the shell prompt on the next line, the program printed a line and ended normally. Pause now and predict: what will happen if I remove \n from the string? (Good — make a mental note.)

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment (4–6 min)
tasks.narratorGuide:
Connect: We'll edit one line: the printf string literal. Observe: Read the string and punctuation carefully — double quotes, backslash n, semicolon. Change: Replace "Hello, World!
" with a personalized message such as "Hello, Cohortia Learner!
" and save. Test: Compile and run: clang greeting.c -o greeting && ./greeting — you should see your message. Then remove the 
, compile and run again. Observe that the shell prompt appears on the same line as your program output. Explain: The newline moves the cursor; without it, subsequent terminal output continues on the same line. Pause and write down what you saw.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate (4–8 min)
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: We're adding a simple variable to practice formatted output. Observe: A string variable uses const char star name equals double-quote your-name double-quote semicolon. Change: Replace the existing printf with two lines: one that sets name and one that uses printf with %s. Test: Compile and run. You should see the exact same greeting, but constructed from a variable. Explain: Using variables lets you change data in one place and reuse it. Extend: Try changing name and recompiling to see how output updates.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend (3–5 min)
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: Errors are useful — they point to syntax issues. Observe: Remove the semicolon at the end of the printf line and run clang greeting.c -o greeting. Change: Read the compilation message carefully. Test: The compiler should print an error referencing an expected ';' or an unexpected token near return. Explain: The error tells you where the parser got confused. Fix the semicolon, recompile, and confirm the program runs. Extend: Try printing two lines or using two printf calls to see how output concatenates.
